newsitem.title: UK: Large explosion heard in Belfast amid unrest.
newsitem.headline: Large explosion heard in Belfast amid unrest.

text.p: A bomb was thrown at a Belfast police station early on Monday morning amid Catholic rioting over the holding of a Protestant Orange order parade in the town of Portadown, police said.
They said police returned gunfire but there were no reports of any injuries.
The bomb, believed to be a hand-held blast bomb, was thrown against the New Barnsley police station in North Belfast during a wave of Catholic rioting in Belfast, Londonderry and other towns.
The explosion echoed around the city centre shortly after midnight amid violent scenes in Catholic Irish nationalist parts of the city.
The violence erupted after police refused to heed Catholic calls to ban an Orange Order march through the Catholic Garvaghy Road area in the flash-point town of Portadown on Sunday morning.

The march went ahead only after one of the biggest police and army operations in recent history saturated Portadown's Catholic enclave to stifle protest and force the march through as quickly as possible.

In Belfast, cars were hijacked and set on fire and the Irish Republican Army claimed responsibility in a statement to a news organisation for the shooting on Sunday of a policewoman in a police vehicle. She was hospitalised with facial injuries.
The IRA, which enjoys support among some section of the 40 per cent Catholic minority, is fighting a 28-year war to end British rule of Northern Ireland.

In one incident, a masked gunman emerged from a side street brandishing what appeared to be an AK-47 assault rifle and fired a volley of shots at a police patrol before disappearing into a side street in the Catholic lower Ormeau road of Belfast, witnesses said.
The unexplained crackle of automatic gunfire was heard in various parts of the city throughout Sunday night and into the early hours of Monday morning.
Police said a volley of shots was fired at police patrol in the Crumlin area and five high-velocity rounds were fired at police in the Springfields area.
Police and ambulance sirens wailed intermittently across the Northern Ireland capital as security and rescue forces rushed from trouble spot to trouble spot, residents said.
Two "spy-in-the-sky" security force helicopters clattered over the capital keeping watch as the demonstrations spread from Catholic neighbourhoods around the city.
Youths torched hijacked cars to draw in police and troops before pelting them with petrol bombs.
Police approached each incident gingerly at first fearing an IRA trap, witnesses said.

Last month the IRA shot dead two policeman in the southern town of Lurgan in an incident which horrified both Ireland and Northern Ireland and led to Britain and Ireland breaking contact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein.
